title: Average 401(k) Balance Hits Record High but Median Saver Has Just $44,000
excerpt: Vanguard's 2026 report shows retirement account balances at all-time highs, but the gap between average and median reveals most workers are far behind.
body:
• The average 401(k) balance hit a record $167,970 at the end of 2025, up 13% from 2024, according to Vanguard's How America Saves 2026 report covering 4.6 million participants.
  • The median balance was $44,115 — less than a quarter of the average — meaning most workers hold far less than the headline figure suggests.
  • Hardship withdrawals rose for the sixth straight year, reaching 6% of participants in 2025, with a median withdrawal of $1,900.
  • Plan participation hit a record 86%, driven by automatic enrollment, which now covers 61% of Vanguard-managed plans compared with just 10% in 2006.

American workers' 401(k) balances reached all-time highs in 2025, powered by a strong stock market and rising contribution rates. But a closer look at the numbers reveals a growing divide: the typical retirement saver has far less than the averages suggest, and more workers are raiding their accounts for emergencies than at any point in the past decade.

Record Balances, Record Gap

Vanguard's 25th edition of How America Saves, released in June 2026, tracked 4.6 million participants in employer-sponsored retirement plans. The average 401(k) balance was $167,970, up from $148,153 in 2024. The median, the point where half of savers are above and half below, came in at $44,115, up 16% from $38,176 in 2024.

Both figures are records. But the four-to-one gap between them tells the real story. Vanguard itself places its own average at roughly the 75th percentile, meaning three out of four participants hold less. One in four had less than $10,000 saved. Just 35% held more than $100,000.

Applied to a standard 4% annual withdrawal rate, the median balance of $44,115 would generate roughly $147 per month in retirement income — a figure that underscores the distance between account balances and retirement security.

How Balances Break Down by Age

The age-by-age data from Vanguard shows the expected pattern of balances growing over a career, but also reveals how far most workers remain from recommended savings targets.

Workers under 25 held an average of $7,259 and a median of $2,234. The 25-to-34 age bracket averaged $50,261, with a median of $18,732. Workers aged 35 to 44 had an average of $120,742 and a median of $46,919. The 45-to-54 bracket averaged $214,991 with a median of $78,730. Workers aged 55 to 64 — the peak saving years — averaged $305,006, with a median of $107,269. For those 65 and older, the average was $330,186 and the median $103,202.

Fidelity's separate data, broken down by generation, paints a similar picture. Gen Z 401(k) holders averaged $18,000, millennials $82,600, Gen X $215,600, and baby boomers $260,300.

More Workers Tapping Savings Early

Even as overall balances climbed, the share of workers taking hardship withdrawals rose for the sixth consecutive year. About 6% of Vanguard participants initiated a hardship withdrawal in 2025, up from 5% in 2024 and triple the pre-pandemic rate. The median withdrawal amount was $1,900.

"Even in the last few years here with rising interest rates, rising inflation, consumer debt at an all-time high — we're still seeing very strong retirement savings behaviors."

— Jeffrey Clark, Head of Defined Contribution Research, Vanguard

Vanguard researchers noted that participants taking multiple withdrawals are effectively using their retirement plans as emergency savings — a pattern that can permanently erode long-term account growth. Broader survey data from the Employee Benefit Research Institute found that 65% of workers describe debt as a problem, and nearly one in three carries more than $25,000 in non-mortgage debt.

Automatic Enrollment Is Driving Participation

Plan participation reached a record 86% in 2025, a milestone Vanguard attributes largely to the spread of automatic enrollment. Sixty-one percent of Vanguard-managed plans now automatically enroll new hires, compared with just 10% in 2006. By reframing the decision as opt-out rather than opt-in, employers have significantly boosted participation rates.

The average total savings rate — combining employee and employer contributions — also hit a record at 12.1%, landing within Vanguard's recommended range of 12% to 15%. Employer matching contributions averaged 4.7%. But worker contributions slipped modestly, with the median deferral rate falling to 6.6% from 6.7% in 2024.

The Confidence Gap

Despite record balances, retirement confidence is declining. Only 64% of Americans said they feel confident about having enough money for a comfortable retirement, down from the prior year, according to EBRI's 2026 survey. Northwestern Mutual's 2026 study found that Americans believe they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably — a benchmark the median 401(k) saver is roughly 33 times short of reaching.

The IRS raised the annual 401(k) contribution limit to $24,500 for 2026, with an $8,000 catch-up allowance for workers 50 and older and an $11,250 "super catch-up" for those aged 60 to 63 under the SECURE 2.0 Act. But those higher ceilings disproportionately benefit high earners: 52% of participants earning $150,000 or more used catch-up contributions, while fewer than 1% of those earning under $30,000 did.

The data suggests that the 401(k) system is succeeding at expanding access through automatic enrollment but struggling with adequacy — the question of whether workers are actually saving enough to fund a secure retirement.
nri_angle: For Indian American professionals, who disproportionately work in tech and finance with employer-matched 401(k) plans, the data underscores the importance of maximizing contributions and catch-up provisions.
